notable_claims: UNL's Computing Resource Center eliminated alt.* newsgroups citing lack of resources, though content was a major factor.
The NCSA email policy permitted searches and punishment for users who criticized the NCSA or University in email.
There is debate over whether electronic political speech on institutional networks constitutes an illegal 'contribution-in-kind' under campaign law.
classification.summary: This is an abstract for the Computers and Academic Freedom (CAF) News digest issue 02.19. It summarizes eleven items concerning network censorship at universities, the legal status of electronic speech as political contributions, and privacy policies regarding email and FTP logging.
classification.title: Article 0 -- Abstract of CAF-News 02.19

notable_claims: The alt.* hierarchy was removed on March 2, 1992.
Official reasons for removal were resource-based, but internal discussions involved state pornography laws.
The UNL Academic Senate Executive Committee voted on April 6, 1992, to request the restoration of the ALT network.
classification.summary: The University of Nebraska-Lincoln (UNL) Computing Resource Center abruptly removed the Usenet alt.* news hierarchy, citing resource constraints. Critics and students argued the move was actually motivated by content control regarding pornography and non-educational use. Following lobbying from students, alumni, and the Electronic Frontier Foundation, the UNL Academic Senate voted to request the restoration of most alt.* groups.
classification.title: SUMMARY AND UPDATE: alt.* Removal at UNL

identity.subject: Article 1--File 7--SUMMARY AND UPDATE: alt.* Removal at UNL

notable_claims: Federal and state regulations on 'contributions-in-kind' may be used to justify the suppression or monitoring of personal political expression on institutional computers.
There is a disparity between how physical spaces (cafeterias, hallways) and electronic spaces are treated regarding permissible personal political activity.
classification.summary: Jim Warren argues that personal political speech, press, and assembly should be protected on institutional computer networks just as they are in physical spaces. He questions why electronic communication is treated differently than voice or paper conversations regarding corporate/institutional 'in-kind' contribution regulations. The post highlights a tension between campaign finance laws and the emerging use of networked computers for personal expression.
classification.title: Article 2--File 5--First Amendment semi-void in electronic frontier ??

identity.subject: Article 2--File 5--First Amendment semi-void in electronic frontier ??

notable_claims: The publication EMMA campaigned to get Usenet newsgroups banned at German universities.
University administrations banned sex-related groups and alt.sexual.abuse.recovery.
Users were encouraged to act as informers against colleagues by spying on their directories.
classification.summary: A report describes the banning of various Usenet newsgroups at several German universities following a campaign by the publication 'EMMA'. The effort encouraged students and faculty to spy on colleagues' directories to identify users of banned groups. Banned content included sexual groups as well as 'alt.sexual.abuse.recovery'.
classification.title: Netnews suppression in Germany

notable_claims: Student Codes often prohibit institutional censorship even in university-owned media.
Public universities are generally legally required to keep student publications free of screening and retaliation.
The Public Forum Doctrine may apply to campus mail systems and other school facilities.
classification.summary: A discussion thread regarding whether universities can restrict students from posting 'hate newsitems' via campus network access. Carl Kadie argues that university-owned computer media should be treated like other student media, which are generally protected from institutional censorship by Student Codes and the First Amendment.
classification.title: College policies on hate messages needed

identity.subject: Article 4--Re: College policies on hate messages needed

notable_claims: The National Security Archive sought to prevent the erasure of Reagan-era White House email tapes.
There is a debate over whether email constitutes an official record or an informal communication similar to a phone call.
Digital records are susceptible to tampering by 'crackers', potentially affecting future historical accuracy.
classification.summary: Barry Margolin discusses a Scientific American article regarding the National Security Archive's efforts to prevent the erasure of White House email backup tapes. The discussion centers on whether electronic mail should be classified as official government records under the Federal Records Act. Margolin notes the tension between the informal nature of email and its importance for historical accountability, specifically citing Iran-Contra era data.
classification.title: Article 5--Email as "official" government correspondence

notable_claims: The CAF Archive served as an electronic library for information on computers and academic freedom available via FTP and email.
EFF provided its internal computer rules as a model for other organizations to use.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie provides an update on the CAF Archive, an electronic library hosted by the Electronic Frontier Foundation. The update lists new additions to the archive, including a review of Jonathan W. Emord's book on technology and the First Amendment, ACLU handbook excerpts regarding student rights, and EFF's own computer use policies.
classification.title: Recent Changes to the Computers and Academic Freedom (CAF) Archive

identity.subject: Article 6--Re: Recent Changes to the Computers and Academic Freedom (CAF) Archive

notable_claims: The University of New Mexico maintained a public FTP directory (/ethics) containing computer policy documents from numerous academic institutions.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie shares a directory listing and readme file for an anonymous FTP archive hosted at the University of New Mexico. The archive contains a collection of computer use policies from various universities and institutions dating from 1989 to 1991.
classification.title: Policy archive at University of New Mexico

identity.subject: Article 7--Policy archive at University of New Mexico

notable_claims: The 'anonymous' FTP login name led some users to believe their actions were not being logged.
Logging is presented as a necessary tool to prevent the total shutdown of public archives due to misuse.
Many FTP sites performed logging without notifying users.
classification.summary: Jim Lick discusses the implementation of transaction logging on an FTP archive at UCSB to prevent abuse and illegal uploads. He describes the tension between user expectations of anonymity (via the 'anonymous' login) and the administrator's need for security and policy enforcement. The post details the transition from silent logging to providing explicit notices to users upon login.

notable_claims: Professor David Kennedy claimed the parody constituted sexual harassment and created a hostile academic environment.
Professors Dershowitz, Fried, and Nesson argued that lack of respect for dignity is not sufficient grounds for disciplining authors under the First Amendment.
classification.summary: A UPI news report describes a conflict at Harvard Law School over a parody of the late Professor Mary Joe Frug published in the Harvard Law Revue. Professor David Kennedy argued for disciplinary action against students, citing sexual harassment and a hostile environment. Conversely, professors Alan Dershowitz, Charles Fried, and Charles Nesson defended the authors' First Amendment rights to free speech.
classification.title: Article 9--UPI story: Parody splits Harvard Law faculty

identity.subject: Article 9--UPI story: Parody splits Harvard Law faculty

notable_claims: The Alabama state legislature passed a law banning gay and lesbian student unions from state schools.
The Auburn student government association denied recognition to the Auburn Gay and Lesbian Alliance on Biblical grounds.
classification.summary: Brian McConnell reports on a legislative move in Alabama to ban gay and lesbian student unions from state schools following a dispute at Auburn University. He urges students on SGANet to discuss a statement condemning the erosion of free speech and assembly rights. The post highlights the intersection of student activism, civil liberties, and early networked communication.
classification.title: Article 10--Auburn University

notable_claims: The NCSA email policy was allegedly created ex post facto to justify searches of a student employee.
University legal counsel opposed broadening privacy policies to include computer files due to concerns over increased university liability.
The restrictive NCSA policy permitted punishment for faculty, students, and researchers who criticized the University or NCSA in emails.
organizations: Campus-Wide Committee on Computing and Networking
classification.summary: Carl Kadie reports on the aftermath of a 1991 National Center for Supercomputer Applications (NCSA) policy that permitted searches and punishment for users criticizing the university or NCSA via email. While a representative campus committee drafted a more protective 'Protection of Electronic Mail and Files' statement, the University Office of Campus Legal Counsel stalled its adoption to avoid increasing liability. The original restrictive NCSA policy remained in force as of April 1992.
classification.title: Article 11--One year later: NCSA email and University computer privacy policies

identity.subject: Article 11--One year later: NCSA email and University computer privacy policies
